XIV, "get full plate though"; the whole of fig. B.1 with its frame, drawn with PhotoCraft).
plays.credit: After the plate in C. Smith, 'Actors with Bird-Masks on Vases', Journal of Hellenic Studies 2 (1881), pl. XIV, fig. B.1 (text pp. 309-314): an Attic black-figure chous attributed to the Gela Painter, c. 510-490 BC, from the Burgon collection; London, British Museum 1842,0728.787 (B 509; Beazley Archive 330555). Scan: JSTOR Early Journal Content, on Zenodo.
plays.license: Public domain (published 1881). The Zenodo copy is marked CC0.
plays.crop: The whole of fig. B.1: the piper, the two dancers, the branches, and the panel's frame as painted (the bars along the top, the chain bands down the sides with their ruled lines, the ground line, and the red lines above and below). Left out: fig. A and the small outline drawings of the two vases on the same plate.
plays.alt_text: A bearded piper in a long cloak plays the double pipes; before him two bearded men dance to the right in bird masks with red crests and beaks, wings strapped to their arms, among branches of ivy
plays.shows: Thematic: a comic chorus dressed as birds, some sixty years before Birds (414 BC), not a scene of the play. Smith read the dancers as actors in bird masks and set them beside the bird chorus of Aristophanes and the earlier Birds of Magnes.
plays.method: Coloured plate, black figures (printed olive) on clay, a silhouette as Cyclops (John's choice), every image step in PhotoCraft (photocraft-cli 0.2.0: crop, enlargement, grey, channel mixes for the clay, the red and the white page, blurs, Motion Blur along the strokes and along the beards' hatching, Maximum and Minimum filters, thresholds), numpy only combining its masks: the clay gives the outline; the black solid with its incisions open, breaks in the thinnest joined; the added red as its own path in the plate's red (John); the right dancer's strokes in black pigment as thin clay lines (John); the incised spots clay; potrace. tools/birds.py.
plays.result: Approved by John on the first pass, 2026-10-12, after a style test (a mask and the piper's hands; the red matched to the plate's, John). About an hour and twenty minutes. No outside review; the credit checked against Smith's text (JHS 2, 309-314), the British Museum's collection record (1842,0728.787: chous, Gela Painter, 510-490 BC, bought from Thomas Burgon 1842) and the Beazley Archive (vase 330555: B509, Gela Painter, 550-500 BC, ABV 473, Para 214).

plays.author: aristophanes
plays.title: Lysistrata
plays.proposed_subject: Five women carrying water jars at a fountain, a chorus of women (John's pick, 2026-10-08: 'do water carriers, and include them all. It's a CHORUS'; the fountain house out). Drawn with PhotoCraft. A first attempt, two dancers from the round dance on Furtwängler-Reichhold I Taf. 17/18 (sweep 2 code 35m), was dropped by John the same day over their clasped hands ('THe hands are the real issue. let's find another image').
plays.credit: After the plate in E. Gerhard, Auserlesene griechische Vasenbilder IV (Berlin, 1858), Taf. CCCVIII, 2 (text pp. 79-80, 'Hydrophoren'): an Attic black-figure hydria from Vulci, c. 530-520 BC, formerly in the Feoli collection, Rome, now Würzburg, Martin von Wagner Museum L 304. The plate is signed 'Lith. Atelier v. A. Schütze in Berlin'. Scan: Heidelberg University Library.
plays.license: Public domain (published 1858). Heidelberg labels the scan with the Public Domain Mark 1.0 (the volume's IIIF manifest, checked 2026-10-08).
plays.crop: The five women with their jars, whole. Left out: the fountain house at the left (the first woman's heel, which stands against its basin, cut straight along it), the painted names, the frame and the ground line under the feet. The plate's upper picture (fig. 1: the vase's shoulder, Herakles and the lion) is not drawn.
plays.alt_text: Five women in long patterned dresses, three carrying water jars on their heads, meet at a fountain
plays.shows: Related to the play: Athenian women fetching water at a fountain, the type of the chorus of old women who carry jars of water up to the Acropolis to douse the old men's fire. The vase does not show the play; the names on it are the women's own (Anthyle, Rhodon, Hegesila, Myrtale).
plays.method: Coloured plate, black figures on clay, a silhouette as Seven Against Thebes, every image step in PhotoCraft (photocraft-cli 0.2.0: crop, enlargement, grey, a warm channel by the Channel Mixer, blurs, Motion Blur along the strokes, Maximum and Minimum filters, thresholds), numpy only combining its masks: the clay gives the outline; the black solid, with its incisions open (the finest on the plate smoothed along their own direction) and the added white of the skin; the faces' lines from the plate; the arms and hands outlined from the skin's smoothed shape; John's traces of the lowered hands laid in as drawn; every line's edge smoothed; potrace. tools/lysistrata.py, tools/lysistrata_traces.json.
plays.result: Approved by John on the fourth pass, 2026-10-09 ('Approved'), after he asked for better hands and smoother lines, traced the lowered hands himself in PhotoCraft, and had a pinky closed and a blot of ink taken out. About four and a half hours' work over two days, with the Falerii attempt. No outside review; the credit checked against Gerhard's text (pp. 79-80), the plate's signature, Wikimedia Commons (ArchaiOptix's photo of Würzburg L 304: the same pictures and inscriptions, findspot Vulci), the American School's booklet Women in the Athenian Agora (fig. 3: 'Würzburg, Martin von Wagner Museum 304', c. 530 BC), and the Feoli collection's sale to Würzburg in 1872. The Beazley Archive's search did not answer (Commons gives BAPD 306484, not checked). Gerhard reads ΗΕΓΕΣΙΛΑ as Telesilla.

plays.author: aristophanes
plays.title: Women at the Thesmophoria
plays.proposed_subject: The parody of Telephus (689 ff.), the whole of side A of Würzburg H 5697 (John, 2026-10-15: 'use the Würzburg scene for Women at the Thesmophoria')
plays.status: Drawn with PhotoCraft 2026-10-14/15, approved by John 2026-10-15 (pass 4) as Aristophanes' home figure; made the play's plate the same day (John), in place of the Getty krater, which went to the Aristophanes author page
plays.credit: After the Apulian red-figure bell-krater Würzburg, Martin von Wagner Museum H 5697, from Rome, acquired 1977 (CVA Würzburg 4, Deutschland 71, ed. G. Güntner, 1999, pp. 13-14, pl. 4, 1-4, Beilage 2, 1; A. Kossatz-Deissmann, 'Telephus travestitus', in Tainia, Festschrift R. Hampe, 1980, 281 ff., pl. 60-61; RVAp I 65 no. 4a; E. Csapo, Phoenix 40, 1986, 379 ff.), side A: the Kinsman on the altar with the wineskin 'baby' and the knife, the woman with the skyphos. Schiller Painter, about 370 BC (CVA). Photographs: ArchaiOptix (Wikimedia Commons). Drawing traced from the photographs and changed.
plays.license: ArchaiOptix's photos CC BY-SA 4.0 (Commons file pages, checked 2026-10-14). The drawing traces only the ancient painting, which is public domain, so it carries no licence (John, 2026-10-08, as for Acharnians); the photographer is credited. No old plate of the vase exists: it came to light in the 1970s (CVA: 'Aus Rom. Erworben 1977'; first published 1980).
plays.crop: The whole of side A (John, 2026-10-14): both figures, the altar with its base, the hanging mirror, the knife and the skyphos. The egg bands above and below the picture are left out; the floor is cut along the top of the band's clay strip, except under her feet, which John drew down to the strip's lower edge.
plays.alt_text: The Kinsman, kneeling on a blood-stained altar, threatens a wineskin dressed as a baby with a knife; Mika, in an old woman's mask, holds out a bowl for its blood
plays.shows: The play itself, as the vase is read: the Kinsman, caught at the festival, seizes a 'baby' that turns out to be a wineskin and threatens it on the altar (689 ff.), a parody of Euripides' Telephus; Mika asks for a bowl to catch its blood (754-755 in the repo's Hall-Geldart text, where she is the First Woman, called Mikka at 760). Kossatz-Deissmann read it as a phlyax farce; Taplin, Green and others as the Thesmophoriazusae itself (CVA).
plays.method: Two photos, one drawing, every image step in PhotoCraft (photocraft-cli 0.2.0): the vase and both cameras fitted together (tools/vase_unroll.py; EXIF 50 mm; the egg band's lower edge, 03's outline, points matched; the two flats agree within 1 px); photo 04 laid onto a flat with the rings straight and the meridians upright (as Wasps). Clay by red less blue; lines by local contrast redrawn along their centres; his hair as paint; faces at their own shape with his stubble's dots; the blood as a wash; her back foot's toes from the two photos averaged; John's marks in three PhotoCraft rounds laid in as he drew them (tools/mika_marks*_*.png); potrace. tools/mika.py.
plays.result: Approved by John on pass 4, 2026-10-15, after three rounds of his marks (about five hours over two days, the source search included): 'the feet (toes specifically) need to be traced clearly'; a second pass on the dress's finer lines, for which he set the photo's levels and drew them in blue; his green erasures (the knife's outlines, her soles); round 2 'additive' (fainter lines and joins); round 3 her pupil, the veil spot and the altar's zigzag ('Replace, keep dots'). No outside review.
plays.superseded: The Getty krater 96.AE.113 (tools/thesmophoriazusae.py, thesmophoriazusae.svg, approved 2026-10-12), the play's plate until 2026-10-15; now the Aristophanes author page's figure, and its crowned king the home figure (see the playwrights list). Earlier: The 2026-10-02 drawing of Mika alone (old woman with skyphos), traced from photo 04 before PhotoCraft: The old woman only, read as Mika (the play's First Woman, called Mikka at 760; the Commons record says 'old woman with skyphos'). The blade of Mnesilochus' knife, which touches her bowl's rim, is cut away along the blade's edge; Mnesilochus, on the altar, is left out.

plays.author: aristophanes
plays.title: Frogs
plays.proposed_subject: The whole of side A of the Apulian bell-krater Cleveland 1989.73: a colossal bust of Dionysos, his thyrsos and vine over his shoulder, between two comic actors, one reaching for grapes, one holding a large skyphos (John's pick, 2026-10-09: Plate Picks 37-Sa, "better because it has comic actors"; the whole side, 2026-10-12; drawn with PhotoCraft 2026-10-12). The earlier proposal, Dionysus as a traveller with a frog motif, was not sourced.
plays.credit: After the Apulian red-figure bell-krater Cleveland Museum of Art 1989.73, side A, attributed to the Choregos Painter, about 390-380 BC (Beazley Archive 1002927; John L. Severance Fund). Photographs: Cleveland Museum of Art (Open Access). Drawing traced from the photograph and changed.
plays.license: The museum's photos CC0 (Open Access; the record's share_license_status, checked 2026-10-12). The drawing traces only the ancient painting and carries no licence.
plays.crop: The whole of side A: the vine with its grapes along the top (under the rim's laurel band), the left actor reaching for a bunch, the thymiaterion at the far left, the bust of Dionysos, and the right actor in his shaggy suit holding the skyphos, on his block, with his tail. Left out: the handles' ornaments, the laurel and meander bands, the black ground. The left actor's costume phallus is drawn as painted (John, 2026-10-09: no censorship).
plays.alt_text: The bust of Dionysos in a wreath and fillet, a vine with grapes above, between two comic actors in masks: on the left one reaches up for a bunch of grapes, on the right one in a shaggy white suit holds out a large cup
plays.shows: Thematic only: the vase is no scene of the play. Dionysos is the hero of Frogs and the god of the theatre, and the two comic actors stand for comedy at his festival; the vase is some fifteen years later than Frogs (405 BC). The museum reads the scene as a bust of Dionysos and comic actors; the right actor's shaggy suit is painted in added white.
plays.method: Red-figure photo taken off the vase (tools/vase_unroll.py): the profile and three of the museum's cameras (the main view, the right handle turned to the camera, side A from above; no EXIF, the focal length fitted at 20000 px) fitted to the meander band, the outline and points matched by SIFT; the flat keeps the rings straight and the meridians upright. Every image step run in PhotoCraft (photocraft-cli 0.2.0), numpy only combining its masks and measuring: the scene by red less blue, the outline on the ground outside the clay; lines by local contrast along their centres, the faces near half maximum; Dionysos's curls as ink over stepped washes; the left actor's hair and goatee a near-black wash; the white suit's tufts as a stepped grey wash past the outline; the grapes' dots as ink; John's lines laid in; potrace. tools/frogs.py.
plays.result: Approved by John on the fourth pass, 2026-10-12, after his notes on the style test (the actor's hair and goatee just short of ink, the grape dots ink, the faces' finer lines, Dionysos's curls darker round the wreath, the vine as clay with an outline) and on passes 1-3 (his lines in PhotoCraft twice; the suit's outline with its tufts over the ground; the cloak's black crisp ink, its part by the floor paint). About three hours, less a pause. No outside review; the credit checked against the museum's record and the Beazley Archive's (1002927: Apulian red-figure with added colour, bell-krater; CVA Cleveland 2, pls. 92-93).

plays.author: aristophanes
plays.title: Assemblywomen
plays.proposed_subject: Three comic actors on a stage before a door: the old man Philotimides and the old woman Charis holding a dish of cakes between them, and the slave Xanthias hiding a stolen cake (John's pick, 2026-10-12: Plate Picks 38-8Ma, Heydemann, Hallisches Winckelmannsprogramm 9 (1884), Taf. I; drawn with PhotoCraft 2026-10-12/13). The earlier proposal, a disguised assembly speaker, was not sourced.
plays.credit: After Taf. I in H. Heydemann, Vase Caputi mit Theaterdarstellungen (Neuntes Hallisches Winckelmannsprogramm, Halle, 1884), pp. 4-5, traced from the vase by Giulio Jatta: an Apulian red-figure bell-krater from Ruvo attributed to the Choregos Painter, about 380-370 BC, Milan, Civico Museo Archeologico A 0.9.2841 (Trendall, Phlyax Vases no. 45). Scan: Heidelberg University Library.
plays.license: Public domain (published 1884). Heidelberg University Library marks the volume with the Public Domain Mark 1.0 (IIIF manifest, checked 2026-10-12).
plays.crop: The whole scene as the plate prints it: the half-open double door, the hanging jug, Philotimides, the bench, Charis with the dish, Xanthias, and the stage on its three posts (John). Left out: the painted names above the actors (John), the vase's frame line under the stage, and the plate's margins. The costume phalluses drawn as printed (John, 2026-10-09: no censorship).
plays.alt_text: Three masked comic actors on a stage before a half-open studded door, a jug hanging above: an old man in a short tunic and an old woman in a long veiled cloak hold a dish of cakes between them over a bench, each holding up a morsel; behind her a bald, bearded slave turns away, a hand at his mouth
plays.shows: Thematic only: the vase names no play. Stock comic types, an old man, an old woman and a slave, on a stage of the kind Assemblywomen was played on; the play has old women fighting over a young man and a feast at its end. Heydemann (pp. 4-5) reads a comedy scene: Philotimides (with a string of figs) and Charis hold a dish of cakes and fruit, and the slave Xanthias, behind her, hides a cake he has stolen in the folds of his tunic. The museum calls it the Cratere dei Ghiottoni (the gluttons' krater).
plays.method: Contour plate, pen lines on cream paper with no black ground, from Heidelberg's largest scan; every image step run in PhotoCraft (photocraft-cli 0.2.0), numpy and scipy only combining its masks, measuring and laying in John's marks: the lines at a share of the way from the paper to their core (paler than Persians'), then redrawn along their centres at their printed width smoothed along them, at 1.6 plate px (John: "crisp and not staticy", and heavier than 0.8, which looked "too much like a pencil drawing"); Xanthias's beard as a stepped grey wash (John: brushstrokes, as on other comedy plates); the door's studs and Xanthias's hem band solid; the vase's frame line, the painted names and smudges dropped; the figures' area by the sealed watershed, John's ground areas by number; clay on the dark theme; John's PhotoCraft marks (all blue, ink) on pass 3; traced at 7200 px tall; tools/ecclesiazusae.py.
plays.result: Approved by John on the fourth pass, 2026-10-13, after a style test, his ground calls by number on pass 1, the lines redrawn crisp and the studs solid on pass 1, the heads redrawn and an A/B of three line weights on pass 2, and one round of his marks in PhotoCraft on pass 3. About four hours over two sittings (an evening and a morning). No outside review; the credit checked against Heydemann's text (pp. 3-5, Heidelberg OCR) and the museum's record (Lombardia Beni Culturali, SIRBeC G0560-00014, which gives the inventory number, the attribution, the date and Trendall, Phlyax Vases p. 38 no. 45).

plays.author: aristophanes
plays.title: Wealth
plays.proposed_subject: Plutus, the god of wealth, an old man with white hair and beard holding a sceptre and a cornucopia (John's pick, 2026-10-08: Plate Picks 39-Ba, Élite III pl. LVIII; 2026-10-10: drawn with PhotoCraft, titled as the Élite reads it).
plays.credit: After the plate in C. Lenormant and J. de Witte, Élite des monuments céramographiques III (Paris, 1858), pl. LVIII (text pp. 121 and 172), after Monumenti inediti dell'Instituto I, pl. IV: an Attic red-figure hydria from Nola attributed to the Painter of London E 183, about 430 BC, London, British Museum 1868,0606.8 (E 183; Beazley Archive 215772). The Élite names the figure Plutus; the museum reads him as Hades (Pluto). Scan: Heidelberg University Library.
plays.license: Public domain (published 1858). Heidelberg labels the scan with the Public Domain Mark 1.0 (the volume's IIIF manifest, checked 2026-10-10).
plays.crop: Plutus alone, the figure at the left end of the frieze, the whole figure with his sceptre. Left out: the rest of the frieze (Triptolemos in his chariot with Demeter, Persephone, Hekate and two more women), the black ground and the panel's frame.
plays.alt_text: An old man with white hair and a white beard, in a long pleated robe and a mantle, holding a long banded sceptre and a large horn of plenty, its mouth crowned with leaves and a shell
plays.shows: A character of the play in another story, not a scene of it: Plutus (Wealth), the god the play is about, at the sending out of Triptolemos; on the vase he can see, where in the play he is blind until healed. The Élite (pp. 121, 172) names him Plutus, the old man with white hair holding the sceptre and the horn of plenty; the British Museum reads him as Hades/Pluto, the Beazley Archive as Hades. John (2026-10-10): titled as the Élite reads it.
plays.method: Coloured plate, red figures on black, a double plate printed upright: the left page's part of the panel squared (its top, bottom and left edges fitted as lines); every image step run in PhotoCraft (photocraft-cli 0.2.0), numpy only combining its masks and measuring: the black ground gives the figure's area, with walls along the sceptre's edges where it crosses the ground, so its black bands stay paint; the added white of the hair and beard (light and not red) drawn as white paths, outlined on the ground by a path the dark theme hides (John); the eye drawn on points read off the plate; every outline drawn on the black ground outside the clay; the line weight kept at pass 1's; a crease in the paper through his head left out; tools/wealth.py.
plays.result: Approved by John on the second pass, 2026-10-10, after he chose the hair's treatment (white paths, with a black outline at the top in day mode only) and asked for one line in the sceptre's head to go. About forty minutes' work, the credit included. No outside review; the credit checked against the Élite's plate list (p. vj) and text (pp. 121, 172), the British Museum's record (1868,0606.8: from Nola, bought from Alessandro Castellani; cites Él. Cér. iii pl. 58) and the Beazley Archive (215772: ARV2 1191.1; cites Élite III pl. 58).

playwrights.alt_text: The Pythia, Apollo's priestess, fleeing in terror with her hands raised

playwrights.alt_text: The shepherd Euphorbos carrying the infant Oedipus on his shoulder, a long spear in his hand
playwrights.shows: Backstory the play turns on: a shepherd, named Euphorbos on the vase, carrying the infant Oedipus, the rescue that the play's last revelation brings to light. Not a scene staged in the play. Chosen by John, 2026-10-02, as Sophocles' home-page figure.
playwrights.method: Furtwängler-Reichhold plate, red figures on the black ground, every image step in PhotoCraft (photocraft-cli 0.2.0), numpy, scipy and scikit-image combining its masks: the close view with its crown filled from the whole plate (SIFT, 0.22 px rms) and levelled; the black ground gives the outline; on the paper outside the panel the spear's printed lines are its outline; the plate's lines by local contrast, redrawn along their centres at the plate's pen width; broken fine lines found again and joined; faces, hands, belt and sandals at their printed width; the child's eye (with iris and pupil), nose and nostril as curves through points read off the plate; Euphorbos' hair, the child's curls and the petasos as `tone` washes; John's PhotoCraft marks on pass 4 laid in (tools/euphorbos_marks_1.png); potrace. tools/euphorbos.py.
playwrights.result: Approved by John on pass 6, 2026-10-12, after a style test and six passes (about four and a half hours): his rulings on the spear, the crop and the washes; then 'Find broken fine lines and complete them', the back of the child's head, the child's nose and eyes ('I want the iris and pupils!'), his blue marks in PhotoCraft on pass 4, and 'there is no cut in' at the child's nape. No outside review; the credit checked against the Furtwängler-Reichhold text (vol. III text, 1932, p. 290: Cab. d. méd. 372, the Achilles Painter's workshop; p. 293 dates the amphora to the end of the 450s; Heidelberg OCR) and JSTOR's record (Beazley Archive 213824).
playwrights.superseded: docs/redesign/drawings/sophocles-oedipus.svg (Oedipus before the Sphinx, Berlin F 2355, photo by Gary Todd, CC0): the phase 1 test. John found it too sparse, and the Sphinx scene misleading about the plot. Then the 2026-10-02 drawing from four ArchaiOptix photos (CC BY-SA 4.0), flattened off the vase (tools/euphorbos.py before 2026-10-12; its record: Drawn 2026-10-02 (second session); redrawn after John's review. John, 2026-10-02, on the second round: 'You flattened it right to my eyes'): John, 2026-10-09: 'that spear is far too long'.

playwrights.proposed_subject: A directly sourced scene from a surviving play
playwrights.status: Redrawn with PhotoCraft, 2026-10-13/15, cut from the whole frieze (iphigenia-in-tauris.svg); approved by John 2026-10-15 (pass 12). Replaces the 2026-10-02 drawing
playwrights.credit: After R. Jaene's lithograph (the plate is signed 'Lith. v. R. Jaene' and 'Druck aus R. Jaene's Kunst-Anst. in Berlin') of the Duke of Buckingham's vase, Archäologische Zeitung 7 (1849), Denkmäler und Forschungen, Taf. XII ('Iphigenia in Tauris. Vasenbild des Herzogs von Buckingham'), with O. Jahn's article. Scan: Internet Archive (Getty Research Institute copy), leaf n156.
playwrights.license: Public domain (published 1849). The Internet Archive item is marked 'Possible copyright status: NOT_IN_COPYRIGHT'.
playwrights.crop: Iphigenia cut from the redrawn frieze along John's own outline (2026-10-14): with the whole tablet, the temple key, its chain and knob, her stole's loops and the drapery hanging from her raised arm. Left out: Pylades, the temple door and steps, the altar behind her, the attendant and her tray. The gap between her hem and her left foot shows the ground, as John's outline draws it.
playwrights.alt_text: Iphigenia, priestess of Artemis, holding out a letter tablet and the temple key
playwrights.shows: The play itself, as O. Jahn identifies the scene in the 1849 publication: Iphigenia handing her letter to Pylades (Iphigenia in Tauris 727 ff.). Jahn records that Welcker read it the other way round, with Iphigenia receiving the letter. The vase's present location was not checked.
playwrights.method: Contour lithograph, fine grey lines drawn like pencil, every image step run in PhotoCraft (photocraft-cli 0.2.0), numpy and scipy only combining its images and measuring: John's Levels on the plate (two steps, 2026-10-13); lines by local contrast with hysteresis, redrawn along their centres at one pen (1.2 scan px), short side branches dropped; breaks joined; the solid black only in the wave band; the checked skirt's hatching a grey wash (John's choice); her eyes, lower lip and chin and the top of her left foot drawn by hand through points read off the plate; John's PhotoCraft marks in eight rounds laid in (tools/iphigenia_tauris_marks_1-8.png: blue lines snapped onto the printed line, blue at half opacity and grey paint a wash, green ground, yellow clay with no ink) and his edits to the ground layer applied last (tools/iphigenia_tauris_ground_edits.png); potrace. tools/iphigenia_tauris.py. The home figure is cut from the frieze along John's outline (tools/iphigenia_tauris_outline.png).
playwrights.result: Approved by John on pass 12, 2026-10-15, after eight rounds of his marks over three days (about ten hours' work, the scan search included). He nearly dropped the plate ('these pencil drawings are just too hard to trace with accuracy'; a search for another subject turned up only plays already drawn), then set its Levels himself. His notes along the way: the eyes ('wonky'; 'We need pupil on both eyes or neither'), the clothing lines ('too many lines look like cracks'; 'it needs to be cleaner and more precise'), the lower lip ('actually two curves'), the broken lines round her left foot, and the ground ('i'm going to erase it in the blue ground layer to be clear'). No outside review.
playwrights.superseded: The 2026-10-02 drawing, Iphigenia alone traced straight from the plate (fine grey lines by local contrast with hysteresis, a least-cost cut along her own lines): Iphigenia with the whole tablet, the temple key, its chain and knob, and her right forearm down its outer edge.

author_page.credit: After the Apulian red-figure bell-krater J. Paul Getty Museum 96.AE.113, side A, attributed to the Cotugno Painter, 370-360 BC (RVAp Suppl. 2, no. 10/46a, as on the Swiss market; Gift of Barbara and Lawrence Fleischman). Photographs: J. author_page.license: The Getty's photos CC0 (Open Content Program; the object's IIIF manifest, checked 2026-10-12). The drawing traces only the ancient painting and carries no licence.
author_page.crop: The whole stage scene: the padded young man with his staff at the left, the actor in the woman's dress with the cloth over the head in the middle, the crowned king with his sceptre at the right; the stage's plank under them (its posts cut at the plank's lower edge). Left out: the handle palmettes, the black ground and the bands. The costume phalluses are drawn as painted (John, 2026-10-09: no censorship).
author_page.alt_text: Three comic actors on a stage: at the left a padded young man with dark hair leans on a staff; in the middle an actor in a woman's dress, a cloth billowing over the head, wears the mask of a white-haired old woman; at the right a crowned king with a white beard and a bird-topped sceptre reaches toward her
author_page.shows: Related to the play by theme only: a phlyax scene. The Getty reads a 'stage-naked' actor (a padded torso over the costume) in a young man's mask with a staff; an actor in a young woman's dress, holding up a cloth that billows over the head, in the white-haired mask of a wrinkled old woman; and a tall crowned actor with a bird-topped sceptre, read as Zeus, reaching toward the woman he takes for young while she eyes the youth. The vase names no play and is some forty years later than Women at the Thesmophoria (411 BC); a man in a woman's dress is what the play's Kinsman is, disguised to spy on the women's festival.
author_page.method: Red-figure photo taken off the vase (tools/vase_unroll.py): the profile and the three Getty cameras (front, left and right profile; no EXIF, the focal length fitted at 30000 px) fitted to the meander band, the outline and points matched by SIFT; the flat keeps the rings straight and the meridians upright, as Wasps. Every image step run in PhotoCraft (photocraft-cli), numpy only combining its masks and measuring: the scene by red less blue; lines by local contrast along their centres at the paint's own width, the faces' finer lines too, the breaks where wear crosses a line closed; the white hair and beards as brushstrokes of PhotoCraft's brush along the paint's grain, tapering, no outline; the king's moustache on John's line, his teeth white; the sceptre's brown shaft and the added yellow as washes; the thinned glaze on the bodies repainted with PhotoCraft's brush along the contours; potrace. tools/thesmophoriazusae.py.
author_page.result: Approved by John on the fifth pass, 2026-10-12, after his notes: the faces' finer lines, the lines through the white beard, the king's teeth white, the moustache round the mouth (he drew the area), and all the white hair as wispy brushstrokes. About four hours. No outside review; the credit checked against the Getty's record (object page and linked-data record: attribution, date, provenance, bibliography, read 2026-10-12).
author_page.chosen: John, 2026-10-15: 'the full apulian bell krator plate for the aristophanes page' (the Getty krater, 96.AE.113)

drawing_format: Each SVG is 1000 units tall with two paths: 'lines' (fill currentColor) and 'body', the figure's area under the lines, class "body" with fill="none", which a page fills with CSS. The body has no holes, except where a scene shows the black ground through it (Philoctetes: between his arms and his body), and lines too thin to hold clay on either side (a goad, a spear) get a narrow clay rim, so the figure reads whole on a dark page. Light pages leave the body transparent; the contact sheet's dark boards fill it with clay and keep the lines dark, as on a red-figure vase (approved by John 2026-10-02; the inverted dark mode looked like a photo negative).
